The person behind them.

What I can do for you.

Don't just take my word for it.

I came out of a commerce degree and ended up designing products.

The short answer is that I kept making things until someone paid me for it. The longer answer is below.

I'm the person who can't leave an interface alone.

I was studying accounts and quietly redesigning every app on my phone in my head. Nobody in my family had heard of UX. It took me an embarrassingly long time to work out that the thing I did for fun was a job someone would pay for.

No design school, and I've stopped apologising for it.

Everything I know came from real work with real deadlines. It left gaps I've had to close deliberately. It also means I've never designed something that didn't have to survive contact with a developer.

I build the things I design.

Four apps live on my phone that I designed and shipped myself. That changes how I work — I argue with constraints instead of drawing around them, and I know what a "small change" actually costs someone.

Four things I do on every project.

I go after the real problem, not the stated one.

Most briefs describe a solution someone already decided on. The useful work happens when you find what's underneath it. On the laundry app, the brief was scheduling. The actual problem was that nobody trusts a stranger with their clothes — and no scheduling screen fixes that.

I'll push back, once, properly.

If I think a decision is wrong I'll say so with a reason, and then I'll build what you decided. You're paying for my judgment, not my agreement — but it's your product, and I'm not going to relitigate a call you've already made.

I design the boring states too.

Empty, loading, error, offline, first-run, the one where the name is too long. These are where products actually feel cheap, and they're what everyone skips. This is the part I'm stubborn about.

I hand over something buildable.

Not a pretty file. Spacing that's consistent, components that behave, states that are specified, motion with actual durations in milliseconds. If your developer has to guess, I haven't finished.
